explanation: The spinal cord receives blood from a single anterior spinal artery (descending from vertebral arteries, supplying the anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries (often from PICA or vertebral arteries, supplying the dorsal columns). Radicular arteries reinforce this supply, with the artery of cervical enlargement providing major additional flow to cervical segments and segmental radicular arteries serving lumbar regions.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior 2/3; posterior spinal arteries supply dorsal columns.

explanation: The spinal cord is a cylindrical structure that extends from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris at approximately the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults. It features cervical and lumbar enlargements corresponding to upper and lower limb innervation, has an anterior median fissure and shallow posterior median sulcus, and is anchored caudally by the filum terminale.
keyConcept: Cylindrical structure; cervical/lumbar enlargements; ends at conus medullaris (L1-L2).

explanation: The pyramidal tract descends and terminates primarily in the ventral horn gray matter of the spinal cord, where corticomotoneuronal synapses occur with lower motor neurons. Approximately 85% of fibers decussate in the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract, controlling distal limb musculature, while the remaining 15% remain ipsilateral as the anterior corticospinal tract influencing proximal and axial muscles.
keyConcept: Terminates in ventral horn; 85% cross as lateral corticospinal tract; 15% remain ipsilateral as anterior corticospinal tract.

explanation: The corticonuclear tract originates from the face area of the primary motor cortex and descends through the genu of the internal capsule to provide bilateral innervation to most cranial nerve motor nuclei. Notable exceptions are the lower facial nucleus (receives predominantly contralateral fibers) and the hypoglossal nucleus (mostly contralateral), which explains the clinical pattern of central facial palsy sparing the forehead.
keyConcept: Bilateral innervation to most cranial nuclei; lower facial and hypoglossal nuclei are primarily contralateral.

explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus in the midbrain and immediately decussates in the dorsal tegmental decussation. It descends in the anterior funiculus to terminate primarily in cervical segments, mediating reflexive turning of the head and eyes toward visual stimuli as part of the extrapyramidal system.
keyConcept: Superior colliculus → decussates → anterior funiculus; mediates visual head-turning reflex.

explanation: The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus in the midbrain, decussates in the ventral tegmental decussation, and descends in the lateral funiculus ending mainly in cervical segments. It facilitates flexion of the upper limbs and inhibits extensor tone, functioning as part of the extrapyramidal motor system that is largely superseded by the corticospinal tract in humans.
keyConcept: Red nucleus → decussates → lateral funiculus; promotes upper limb flexion.

explanation: The cervical spinal cord is supplied by the anterior spinal artery—a single midline vessel formed from vertebral arteries that perfuses the anterior two-thirds of the cord—and paired posterior spinal arteries, often branching from PICA or vertebral arteries, supplying the dorsal columns. The artery of cervical enlargement and other radicular arteries provide critical segmental reinforcement.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery = anterior 2/3; posterior spinal arteries = dorsal columns; radicular arteries reinforce supply.

explanation: Syringomyelia is a chronic progressive disorder characterized by the formation of a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, most commonly in the cervical and upper thoracic regions. As the syrinx expands centrally, it damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers near the central canal first, producing the classic dissociated sensory loss: bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation while proprioception and fine touch remain preserved.
keyConcept: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss—pain and temperature are lost while touch and proprioception are preserved.

explanation: The clinical picture described—fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension of both spoken and written language—is characteristic of Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia. Although classically localized to Brodmann area 22, posterior language association areas including the angular gyrus (area 39) and supramarginal gyrus (area 40) are critically involved in semantic comprehension and phonological processing, and lesions here produce receptive language deficits.
keyConcept: Receptive aphasia involves posterior language areas; semantic and phonological processing occur in angular and supramarginal gyri.

explanation: The prefrontal cortex regulates personality, motivation, emotional behavior, and executive function. Damage to this area—especially the orbitofrontal and dorsolateral regions—produces frontal lobe syndrome characterized by apathy, loss of initiative, emotional blunting, and disinhibition, while primary motor, sensory, visual, and language functions remain intact.
keyConcept: Prefrontal lesions cause frontal lobe syndrome (apathy, personality change) without motor or sensory deficits.

explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb reaches the cerebellum primarily via the cuneocerebellar tract. This pathway relays information from the cuneate nucleus to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying proprioceptive input from the upper limb and upper trunk, analogous to how the dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries lower limb proprioception.
keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries upper limb proprioception to cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle is predominantly an efferent pathway carrying fibers from the dentate nucleus to the thalamus and red nucleus. However, it also conveys the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract, which is the major afferent pathway entering the cerebellum through this peduncle, carrying proprioceptive information from Golgi tendon organs.
keyConcept: Superior peduncle is mainly efferent; anterior spinocerebellar tract is its main afferent component.

explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle is the principal afferent pathway to the cerebellum. It carries the posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract, cuneocerebellar tract, olivocerebellar fibers, vestibulocerebellar fibers, and reticulocerebellar fibers, all conveying sensory and proprioceptive information essential for coordination and balance.
keyConcept: Inferior peduncle is the main afferent route; carries posterior spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, and olivocerebellar fibers.

explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle contains the ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract, which carries unconscious proprioceptive information from the lower limb and trunk. Unlike the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (inferior peduncle), the ventral tract decussates twice (once in the cord, once in the cerebellar white matter) and enters via the superior peduncle.
keyConcept: Ventral spinocerebellar tract enters through the superior cerebellar peduncle.

explanation: The dentate nucleus is the largest and most lateral of the deep cerebellar nuclei, located within the white matter of each cerebellar hemisphere. It receives input from the Purkinje cells of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres (neocerebellum) and is the main output nucleus for cerebellar coordination of voluntary limb movements.
keyConcept: Dentate nucleus = largest, most lateral cerebellar nucleus; output of neocerebellum.

explanation: The dentate nucleus serves as the primary efferent nucleus of the neocerebellum (lateral cerebellar hemispheres). It projects via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral red nucleus and ventral lateral nucleus of the thalamus, relaying information to the motor cortex for coordinated voluntary movements.
keyConcept: Dentate nucleus projects neocerebellar efferents via the superior cerebellar peduncle to thalamus and red nucleus.

explanation: The neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum) is the phylogenetically newest part of the cerebellum, anatomically corresponding to the posterior lobe, specifically the lateral cerebellar hemispheres and the vermis of the posterior lobe. It receives massive cortical input via the pontine nuclei (through the middle cerebellar peduncle) and is essential for planning and coordinating voluntary movements.
keyConcept: Neocerebellum = posterior lobe (lateral hemispheres); coordinates voluntary movement planning.

explanation: The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) consists of the medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle. The crus cerebri is part of the cerebral peduncle in the midbrain (mesencephalon), not the hindbrain, making it the exception among the listed structures.
keyConcept: Hindbrain = medulla, pons, cerebellum, 4th ventricle; crus cerebri is in the midbrain.

explanation: The abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) emerges from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, specifically from the sulcus between the lower border of the pons and the pyramid of the medulla. Its nucleus lies in the caudal pons beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle, contributing to the facial colliculus.
keyConcept: Abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges between pons and pyramid at the pontomedullary junction.

explanation: The trochlear nerve (cranial nerve IV) is unique among cranial nerves because it is the only one to exit from the dorsal surface of the brainstem, specifically just below the inferior colliculus. It then decussates in the superior medullary velum before emerging anteriorly and ascending to innervate the superior oblique muscle.
keyConcept: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to exit from the dorsal surface of the brainstem.

explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is a diamond-shaped depression on the ventral surface of the midbrain, bounded by the cerebral peduncles. Its contents include the tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, and the emerging oculomotor nerves. The anterior perforated substance lies rostral to this fossa, in the floor near the lateral sulcus.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa contains tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, and CN III; anterior perforated substance is anterior to it.

explanation: The cerebellopontine angle is the space at the junction of the pons, medulla, and cerebellum. The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) passes through this angle along with the facial nerve (CN VII) and nervus intermedius. Acoustic neuromas commonly arise here, compressing these structures.
keyConcept: Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) traverses the cerebellopontine angle.

explanation: The fourth ventricle is a diamond-shaped cavity between the cerebellum and the brainstem. It possesses lateral recesses that extend toward the foramina of Luschka. The pineal recess, suprapineal recess, optic recess, and infundibular recess are all features of the third ventricle, not the fourth.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle has lateral recesses; pineal, optic, and infundibular recesses belong to the third ventricle.

explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle contains several important nuclei. The medial eminence overlies the abducens nucleus (CN VI). Just lateral to it is the facial colliculus, a swelling formed by the internal genu of the facial nerve looping over the abducens nucleus.
keyConcept: Medial eminence overlies the abducens nucleus; lateral to it is the facial colliculus.

explanation: The fourth ventricle communicates superiorly with the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), which connects it to the third ventricle. Inferiorly, the fourth ventricle narrows into the central canal of the spinal cord. The lateral recesses lead to the foramina of Luschka.
keyConcept: Superior angle of 4th ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 3rd ventricle.

explanation: The pontomedullary junction (lower border of pons) gives rise to the abducens (CN VI), facial (CN VII), vestibulocochlear (CN VIII), and nervus intermedius nerves. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the exception—it emerges from the lateral aspect of the pons proper, not from the lower border.
keyConcept: Trigeminal nerve (CN V) emerges from the lateral pons; lower border nerves are VI, VII, VIII.

explanation: The brainstem comprises three contiguous structures in ascending order: the medulla oblongata (most caudal), the pons, and the midbrain (mesencephalon). The cerebellum is attached to the dorsal aspect of the brainstem via the cerebellar peduncles but is anatomically distinct and is not considered part of the brainstem proper.
keyConcept: Brainstem = medulla, pons, midbrain; cerebellum is attached but not part of brainstem.

explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) emerges from the medulla as 10-15 rootlets in the preolivary sulcus (anterior median sulcus), located between the pyramid medially and the olive laterally. It exits through the hypoglossal canal to innervate all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except the palatoglossus.
keyConcept: Hypoglossal rootlets lie in the preolivary sulcus between pyramid and olive.

explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) emerges from the postolivary sulcus of the medulla, located lateral to the olive and medial to the inferior cerebellar peduncle. It carries special visceral afferent taste from the posterior third of the tongue, general visceral afferent sensation, and parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland.
keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) emerges lateral to the olive in the postolivary sulcus.

explanation: The abducens nerve (CN VI) emerges at the pontomedullary junction in a position very close to the midline, between the pons superiorly and the pyramid of the medulla inferiorly. Because of this medial location, abducens palsy is a common false-localizing sign of increased intracranial pressure.
keyConcept: Abducent nerve (CN VI) emerges near the midline at the pontomedullary junction.
